cards.front: Why do cells store glucose as large polysaccharides rather than as free glucose molecules?
cards.back: Polysaccharides are large and mostly **insoluble**, so they do not affect the movement of water by osmosis. They are also compact, so a lot of glucose fits in a small space.
cards.hint: Think about what many free sugar molecules would do to the water inside a cell.

cards.front: Why is cellulose strong enough to support plant cell walls?
cards.back: Cellulose is made of **β-glucose** units, so its chains are straight. Hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring chains, and bundles of chains form **microfibrils**.
cards.hint: Compare how the chain shape of cellulose differs from that of starch.

cards.front: Why does glycogen allow glucose to be released faster than starch?
cards.back: Glycogen is more highly **branched**, so it has many chain ends. Enzymes can hydrolyse glucose from many ends at the same time.
cards.hint: Count how many places an enzyme could act at once on each molecule.

cards.back: A **monosaccharide** is a carbohydrate made of one sugar unit, the simplest group. Glucose, fructose and galactose are common examples.
A **glycosidic bond** is a covalent bond between two sugar units. It forms by a condensation reaction.

cards.front: How is a disaccharide such as maltose formed from two monosaccharides?
cards.back: Two glucose molecules join in a **condensation** reaction. A glycosidic bond forms between them and one water molecule is released.
cards.hint: Think about what is lost from the molecules when the new bond forms.

cards.front: What equation shows the formation of maltose from two glucose molecules?
cards.back: $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6(aq)+C_6H_{12}O_6(aq)\rightarrow C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}(aq)+H_2O(l)}$. Each glucose is $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$, maltose is $\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}$, and the water released is $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

cards.front: Why must a disaccharide such as sucrose be split before the body can use it?
cards.back: Most disaccharides are too large to cross cell membranes. They must be hydrolysed into **monosaccharides** first.
cards.hint: Think about what size of molecule can pass through a membrane.

cards.back: **Hydrolysis** is the reverse of condensation. A water molecule is used to break a glycosidic bond, and each break uses one water molecule.
cards.hint: Think about which reaction adds water rather than releasing it.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that starch and cellulose are made of the same form of glucose?
cards.back: Starch is made of **α-glucose**, while cellulose is made of **β-glucose**. This small difference in shape changes the structure and function of each polysaccharide.

cards.front: What two parts make up starch?
cards.back: Starch is a mixture of coiled, unbranched **amylose** and branched **amylopectin**. Both are made of α-glucose units.
A **microfibril** is a bundle of cellulose chains held together by hydrogen bonds. Microfibrils make plant cell walls strong.
cards.hint: Think about how many weak bonds it takes to build a strong structure.

cards.front: Why does cellulose pass through the human gut as fibre rather than being digested?
cards.back: Humans lack an **enzyme** that hydrolyses the bonds between β-glucose units, so cellulose is not broken down.
cards.hint: Consider which enzymes the body makes to break down sugars.
